headline: Antipodes cautious on memory semiconductor names as share prices extrapolate peak-cycle pricing with limited margin of safety
reasoning: Memory remains a largely commoditised product, so even with strong end-demand these businesses have limited control over their own pricing. Share prices already appear to extrapolate peak-cycle pricing far into the future, leaving little room for disappointment. High prices invite capacity additions, and if the industry learns to use memory more efficiently through better software, architecture or compression, demand growth could moderate just as new supply arrives. At current valuations, there is a thin margin of error precisely when expectations are highest.
quote: Memory, a key segment within this hardware complex, has traditionally been deeply cyclical. We acknowledge the current cycle is being supported by plausible structural tailwinds in the form of AI capex build-out. Our caution is more specific. Memory remains a largely commoditised product, so even with strong end-demand these businesses have limited control over their own pricing. The following risks stand out: Share prices already appear to extrapolate peak-cycle pricing far into the future, leaving little room for disappointment. High prices invite capacity additions, and if the industry learns to use memory more efficiently, through better software, architecture or compression, demand growth could moderate just as new supply arrives. Either path could expose the cyclicality that the structural narrative is currently masking. At current valuations, that leaves a thin margin of error precisely when expectations are highest.

headline: China's anti-involution (supply-side reform) policy is a key macro theme but lacks the demand-side stimulus needed to broadly sustain a bull market
reasoning: Anti-involution is effectively anti-excessive competition, similar to supply-side reform seen in 2015. In 2015, 45 consecutive months of negative PPI growth triggered reform; the current episode followed 33 consecutive months of negative PPI. The key difference is that the 2015 reform was paired with demand-side stimulus, creating a major bull market; this time, no significant demand-side stimulus is expected. As a result, low-quality companies that initially rallied on anti-involution expectations may struggle to sustain performance. Antipodes looks for companies that have already generated strong returns through the period of excessive competition, rather than those relying on policy tailwinds alone.
quote: Anti-involution is effectively anti-excessive competition – supply side reform is the best way to describe it. And that's not new in China; it happened in 2015. What triggered it back then was about 45 consecutive months of negative producer price index (PPI) growth. Fast forward to June 2025 when this thematic started to make noise – we'd had 33 consecutive months of negative PPI. A similar situation. The difference from 2015 is that back then the supply side reform was joined with demand side stimulus, which led to a huge bull market in Chinese equities. So far we've had the supply side reform but haven't really had effective demand side stimulus, and we're not expecting significant demand side stimulus either.

headline: Antipodes PM argues EM/Asia is entering a long upcycle driven by valuation, weaker USD, and capital rotation from US mega-caps
reasoning: John Stavliotis argues that emerging markets have underperformed developed markets for 15 years and conditions are now shifting. Key tailwinds include cheap valuations (China at ~13x PE, Indonesia at 25th historical percentile), a rolling-over US dollar (which historically aids EM), improving global growth that is eroding US exceptionalism, and improving commodity prices. He also notes that the Magnificent Seven's market cap is more than twice the entire MSCI EM Index, meaning even modest outflows from US large-caps could have an outsized positive effect on EM equities, supporting a potentially long upcycle.
quote: Emerging market cycles are quite long, and we've been through a quite painful cycle over the last 15 years of underperformance relative to developed markets. We think there are some reasons why that's changing. Valuation is one I've already talked about. The other is the high correlation with US dollar strength and weakness – a weaker US dollar typically helps allocations to EM, and we're starting to see the US dollar roll over. Interest rates and global growth – We are starting to see global growth improve, and really that US exceptionalism, which is what's driven that flow of capital to the US, is starting to at least equalise with higher global GDP growth, and we're seeing that in commodity prices improving. If that continues, we think that EM cycle will be a long cycle on the upside. Another way to put it in context – the amount of money in the Magnificent Seven is currently over two times the value of the MSCI EM Index. So a little bit of money coming out of the US large caps will have a huge effect on Asian equities or emerging market equities, and that's why that cycle can last for quite a long time.

headline: Antipodes cautious on direct investment in Chinese humanoid robot makers, preferring picks-and-shovels component suppliers in less competitive sub-markets
reasoning: In person, the humanoid robots on display were slower and clumsier than their promotional videos suggested. Government subsidies and cheap capital are encouraging every firm with relevant technology to enter humanoid robotics, creating intense competition that makes sustained returns for robot-makers difficult. Antipodes is instead seeking opportunities in component manufacturers—such as actuator suppliers—operating in more consolidated niches.
quote: Investing in the companies that are doing the humanoid robots is probably going to be very hard because of the competition. And we're looking for opportunities in call at the picks and shovels side. So, for example, companies that are providing the actuators or other hardware components to make these robots.
